description:
We are Team UPMASS. We built this game because every guide to space mission design shows you the steps, but never the weight of the choices. Mass over budget. A test that costs two days you don't have. Something gets left behind, and someone lives with that.

We went to NASA's own documents, found that moment, and made it playable. We are four people who wanted this game to exist, so we made it. One mission. Every decision comes back.
summary:
Long space missions face a silent risk: essential vitamins degrade in packaged food over months and years, leaving astronauts vulnerable to nutrient deficiencies without resupply from Earth. NASA's BioNutrients research tested an elegant solution: storing dried yeast spores that crew members can rehydrate in space to produce fresh nutrients on demand.

UPMASS is a fifteen-minute browser game built around that real engineering challenge. You play as an astronaut managing two payloads sharing one soft cargo bag: a yeast nutrient experiment based on BioNutrients-2 and a student-built 1U CubeSat named LANTERN-1.

With strict limits on mass (5.50 kg), volume, power (100 W), crew time, and testing days, every decision forces a real compromise. At mission end, an automated debrief checks your flight against NASA's published BioNutrients-2 engineering requirements, explaining exactly which early trade-offs led to success or failure.
details:
What the Project Does and How It Works

UPMASS is an interactive 3D story game that puts players in charge of the trade-offs behind a real space mission. Rather than presenting space engineering as a series of theoretical flowcharts, the game drops you directly into eight chronological chapters spanning fourteen months of mission preparation and flight.

You play as Sam, an astronaut coordinating cargo for an upcoming International Space Station resupply flight. Two separate research payloads must share a single soft cargo bag (a standard NASA Cargo Transfer Bag):

  1. A biological nutrient production experiment modeled on NASA's BioNutrients-2 investigation. The payload uses genetically engineered yeast stored as dormant dry spores. In orbit, the crew injects sterile water into flexible production packs, mixes them, incubates them, and freezes the final samples for return to Earth.
  2. A 1U student satellite (LANTERN-1) developed under parameters from the NASA CubeSat Launch Initiative. Before flight, the satellite must undergo environmental testing (vibration shake, thermal vacuum bakeout, and day-in-the-life electronics testing) to ensure it poses no risk to the space station or its crew.

The player interacts directly with the physical environment rather than abstract menus. In the cargo staging room, you place packs on an inspection scale, watch the mass counter tick up toward the 5.50 kg limit, and decide what stays and what gets left behind. On orbit, you manage syringe injections, incubator power draw, airlock deployment latches, and freezer storage slots.

What Benefits It Has and Educational Value

Traditional educational resources explain the lifecycle of a space mission as clean, sequential milestones: requirements definition, preliminary design, qualification testing, launch, and operations. In reality, spaceflight engineering is defined by competing budgets and unforgiving constraints.

UPMASS teaches these fundamental aerospace engineering principles by making players experience their consequences:

  • Mass and Volume Budgets (Upmass Constraints): Players understand why every gram matters when payload limits force them to choose between carrying scientific spares or flying satellite test hardware.
  • Concept Maturity Levels (CML): The game introduces JPL's Concept Maturity framework intuitively. Chapter 1 represents CML 1 ("Cocktail Napkin" concept definition in a diner with lead scientist Maren), while Chapter 2 moves to CML 4 ("Point Design" with strict mass, power, and timeline allocations).
  • Verification vs. Schedule Pressure: Players decide whether to skip qualification tests (such as thermal vacuum bakeout or a second shake test) to meet tight delivery deadlines. Skipping a test saves schedule days, but introduces hidden failure risks in orbit.
  • Resource Contention on ISS: In Chapter 4, players operate with a strict 100 W power ceiling and two hours of crew time, learning that running an incubator, downlinking telemetry, and assisting a crewmate cannot all happen simultaneously.
  • Traceable Engineering Debrief: At the end of the game, players receive an itemized evaluation matrix directly derived from NASA's flight requirements for BioNutrients-2. Every red line traces back to a specific decision made in earlier chapters.

The Intended Impact of the Project

The primary goal of UPMASS is to demystify systems engineering for students, educators, and space enthusiasts worldwide.

Aerospace concepts often feel inaccessible due to dense technical jargon and abstract mathematics. By grounding the experience in human characters and tactile interactions, UPMASS allows anyone with a web browser to understand why space missions are designed the way they are.

Because the game runs entirely in client-side WebGL with zero installation, zero account registration, and adaptive graphics settings, it can be played on modest school laptops, mobile devices held horizontally, or high-end desktop workstations. An integrated in-game Glossary and Sources viewer provides direct citations to real NASA documentation, allowing curious players to immediately transition from gameplay to reading authentic NASA technical reports.

Tools, Coding Languages, and Software Used

UPMASS was developed from the ground up as a lightweight, zero-dependency web application:

  • Rendering Engine: Built with three.js (version r160) utilizing WebGL 2. The pipeline features physically based materials (PBR), procedural normal mapping, screen-space ambient occlusion (SSAO), pointer-based depth of field, bloom, and tone mapping inside a cinematic 2.39:1 widescreen frame.
  • Frontend Architecture: Pure vanilla JavaScript (ES modules), HTML5, and CSS3. No heavy frontend frameworks, no bundlers, and no server-side dependencies. Hosted statically at upmass.earth.
  • Audio Synthesis: Real-time dynamic audio engine built with the Web Audio API. Background ambient room tones, procedural hums, and musical pads respond interactively to gameplay states and dialogue cues.
  • Voice Synthesis: Character dialogue was generated offline using Kokoro-82M, an open-source neural text-to-speech model running via the kokoro-onnx runtime engine. Over 280 lines of dialogue were processed through room acoustic simulation filters to match the ambient environment of each scene.
  • Automated Playtesting Bot: An internal development bot (js/dev-bot.js) was engineered to execute automated play-throughs across all branching decision trees, verifying state consistency, audio timings, and debrief matrices across hundreds of permutations.
  • AI Coding Assistance: Claude (Anthropic) was utilized as an engineering assistant for code implementation, dialogue editing, and documentation formatting under team direction.
    • NASA 3D Resources: Reference geometry for the 1U CubeSat and Crew Lock Bag.
    • NASA Earthdata GIBS (Global Imagery Browse Services): Satellite base imagery for the orbital globe view.
    • NASA FIRMS (VIIRS NOAA-20): Real-world active thermal hotspot data for night-side Earth visualization.
    • Poly Haven: CC0 panoramic environment maps for lighting and skybox reflections.

What Makes the Project Creative

UPMASS avoids conventional user interface tropes like multiple-choice dialog trees, floating sliders, and quiz popups. Instead, creativity is embedded directly in physical scene mechanics:

  1. Diegetic Interaction: All critical engineering parameters exist as physical objects inside the 3D room. You check battery levels by looking at a backlit meter on an electronics rack, verify bag mass by reading an industrial bench scale, and make decisions by picking up, toggling, or setting down actual items.
  2. Delayed Consequence Architecture: In many educational games, decisions produce instant feedback. In UPMASS, consequences remain dormant across multiple chapters. Skipping a satellite day-in-the-life test in Chapter 2 seems harmless at first; only in Chapter 5, when deploying the satellite from the station airlock, does a timer glitch prevent the communication antenna from deploying on schedule.
  3. Honest Engineering Ambiguity: There is no "perfect run" where every system succeeds without sacrifice. If you choose to pack 18 nutrient packs for maximum scientific redundancy, you force the student satellite team to eliminate their backup antennas and cut ground verification days. Every outcome reflects real engineering compromises.

Key Engineering Factors Considered by the Team

To maintain authentic scientific rigor, our team structured the game around verified flight constraints:

  • NASA BioNutrients-2 Flight Requirements: The game's final debrief evaluates player performance against exact parameters from NASA's BioNutrients mission standards:
    • Minimum 12 viable returned sample packs for statistical validity.
    • Minimum 30 mL volume of sterile water per production pack.
    • Target production yield of at least 3 micrograms of beta-carotene per mL of sample.
    • Minimum 1.0 mg dry cell weight per sample.
    • Absolute absence of microbial contamination during in-flight hydration.
    • Single pack mass below 250 g and volume below 300 mL to satisfy stowage limitations.
    • 1U standard form factor: 10 cm x 10 cm x 11.35 cm with mass capped at 1.33 kg.
    • Three electrical inhibits required on battery lines to prevent premature RF broadcast or solar panel deployment inside the crewed cabin.
    • Environmental qualification matrix: Random vibration testing to simulate launch acoustics, thermal vacuum bakeout to eliminate toxic material outgassing, and Day-in-the-Life (DITL) verification to ensure deployment timer sequencing works autonomously.
  • Cold Stowage and Thermal Emergency Management: Biological samples must be kept at -80 deg C or -20 deg C post-growth to halt enzymatic degradation. In Chapter 6, the game simulates an ISS cold stowage anomaly (modeled on real MELFI freezer drawer temperature alerts), forcing players to triage which sample packs receive emergency insulation based on whether they flew temperature loggers in Chapter 2.
